items.title: Microsoft identifies months-old bug as a root cause of global outage
items.summary:

The office software giant issued an initial report on Monday that identified three factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of its services: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections , and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own, but, when taken together, they led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives said.

items.title: ‘We’re having to overcome brand America’: Kraft Heinz CEO says made-in-U.S.A. designation is more ‘complicated’ in appealing to Canadian customers
items.summary:
As U.S.-Canadian relations go frosty, one American food brand is having to be more intentional about appealing to its northern neighbors.

Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane said the made-in-the-U.S.A. moniker doesn’t carry the same positive connotation as it did in decades past. As a result, he said, the Chicago- and Pittsburgh-based food giant—behind Jell-O, Lunchables, and Heinz ketchup—is having to tweak its messaging.

“Brand America is not as strong as it once was, and that’s been the case for some time,” Cahillane told Fortune Executive Editorial Director Diane Brady. “We’re having to overcome brand America. Whereas, in the ‘50s, ‘60s, ‘70s, into the ‘80s, brand America was a badge of honor, it’s a little bit more complicated today.” 

Ongoing trade tensions, including a 50% tariff on $20 billion of Canadian goods , have chilled Canadian attitudes towards American productions, as have repeated threats from U.S. President Donald Trump about making Canada the “ 51st state ,” claiming it relies too heavily on the U.S. economically. While Canadians have continued to pour money into U.S. investments , many have also made a concerted effort to boycott American goods in favor of Canadian counterparts. 

In some areas, these boycotts are taking a toll on the U.S. economy. A report from the Canadian government published last month found that despite Canadian visitations to the U.S. beginning to increase, visitations from Canadians are 29% lower as of September 2026 than they were two years ago. According to the…
items.t: ‘We’re having to overcome brand America’: Kraft Heinz CEO says made-in-U.S.A. designation is more ‘complicated’ in appealing to Canadian customers

items.title: Days after Microsoft and the FAA went dark, Chase and Wells Fargo customers can’t get to their money
items.summary:
If you had trouble logging into your bank’s website on Monday, you’re not alone. JPMorgan Chase customers spent much of the day unable to log in or move money, with the bank saying the outage spread from it’s website and app to some branches and to outside apps that connect to Chase accounts. Wells Fargo also confirmed problems with its online banking, and customers at other large banks reported trouble.

Reports started Monday morning and climbed quickly. Downdetector logged nearly 4,500 Chase reports shortly after 1:30 p.m., most of them about website logins. By 2:22 p.m., the count had passed 20,000.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson said. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.” 

Customers described a wider disruption than that statement suggests. Comments on Downdetector mentioned problems with ATMs and in-person systems as well as online banking and Zelle. Some customers opening the Chase app got a message reading , “Some services aren’t available.”

Ashley Lutz 

The problems also reached apps outside the bank. Plaid, which links bank accounts to payment, investing and budgeting apps, said its own network was working normally but that it was seeing connection problems with Chase accounts. Customers trying to link or refresh a Chase account through another app may have gotten errors as a result.

Downdetector listed Chase, Wells Fargo, Capital One and Bank of America among the banks with spikes in outage reports,…
items.t: Days after Microsoft and the FAA went dark, Chase and Wells Fargo customers can’t get to their money

items.title: Oracle CEO admits tech sector made a ‘classic mistake’ not engaging local communities on data centers but sees new strategy to win ‘hearts and minds’
items.summary:
Oracle co-CEO Mike Sicilia says the tech industry made a “classic mistake” in how it sold data centers to the towns asked to host them: “flying people in to say, ‘I’m from HQ, and I’m here to help.’ That’s not how we’re gonna win hearts and minds.”

His comments, at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday, came two weeks after voters turned the midterms into a referendum on the AI buildout. For companies racing to build AI capacity, the bottleneck is now local permission as much as power or chips.

Tech and data-center companies aren’t used to having to make these arguments, he said. “That’s actually not surprising, given many tech company have traditionally been suppliers not operators in local communities,” the AI hyperscaler chief told Fortune ‘s Jeremy Kahn. 

Trane Technologies CEO Dave Regnery pointed out that rhetoric coming out of candidates during campaigns can be different after they get elected. In fact, Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has signaled she will not block data center projects that have already secured permits.

Regnery said educating the public is also key as there are some myths about data centers need to be debunked. The one that especially bothers him is the notion that data centers use too much water. But in reality, most use closed-loop systems, meaning water within a data center is recirculated.

As for the complaint that data centers suck up so much electricity that utilities are hiking rates for customers, Regnery noted that buildings waste about 30% of the energy they pay for, but Trane’s agentic AI controls could get them…
items.t: Oracle CEO admits tech sector made a ‘classic mistake’ not engaging local communities on data centers but sees new strategy to win ‘hearts and minds’

items.title: AI could soon be telling CEOs whom to lay off, Arist CEO Michael Ioffe predicts: ‘The speed of decision making is so much faster’
items.summary:
AI is already fueling workers’ fears of being replaced. Now, one startup CEO predicts it could soon help companies decide whether to lay them off, too.

“We do expect that within the next few years, the majority of significant enterprise shifts, whether it’s products you’re launching, you know, layoffs that you’re making, et cetera, will be recommended by agents,” Michael Ioffe, cofounder and CEO of Arist, said while speaking with Fortune ‘s Kristin Stoller at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

Ioffe’s company uses AI agents to interview employees, comb through company data, and recommend solutions to business problems. Arist already works with more than 15% of the Fortune 500, and its technology can gather insights from thousands of employees in just 72 hours—a process that traditionally requires teams of consultants. Still, he doesn’t envision executives handing over control entirely. 

“At the end of the day, it will always be an executive who is making the final call,” Ioffe said. 

That prediction comes as more companies cite AI when cutting jobs, sometimes drawing accusations of “AI washing,” or blaming technology for cuts made for other reasons. But even when companies genuinely expect AI to replace workers, moving too quickly can backfire. As Stoller previously reported , HR leaders have warned that companies risk losing valuable talent when they cut workers without a clear plan for how AI will replace their work.

For Ioffe, the appeal is speed. When sales fall or a product struggles, companies often spend months and millions of dollars working with…
items.t: AI could soon be telling CEOs whom to lay off, Arist CEO Michael Ioffe predicts: ‘The speed of decision making is so much faster’

items.title: China ‘full stop, is ahead of us’: SpaceX alum building a $13 billion defense startup warns of Beijing’s hypersonic weapons
items.summary:
While Jensen Huang’s resignation has put a renewed spotlight on the U.S.-China race for dominance in chips and artificial intelligence, another technological contest could have even more direct national security implications : hypersonic weapons.

And the U.S. is already trailing behind, according to Andrew Kreitz, cofounder and CFO of Castelion —a $13 billion defense startup focused on developing hypersonic missiles.

“Unfortunately, China, especially, full stop, is ahead of us in hypersonics,” Kreitz told Fortune ’s Andrew Nusca at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, Mich.

The U.S., for its part, has begun fielding its first long-range hypersonic missile system, known as “ Dark Eagle .” China, meanwhile, has been steps ahead for years and “has the world’s leading hypersonic missile arsenal,” according to the U.S. Department of Defense’s 2025 report to Congress.

Kreitz pointed to several reasons for the gap, starting with how the U.S. defense industry develops and builds weapons. He said the Pentagon has often prioritized the most advanced technology without giving enough thought to cost or how easily it can be manufactured. Cost-plus contracts, which reimburse contractors for their expenses, also give companies less incentive to control costs.

The aerospace and defense industry also suffers from failing to test hardware early and often, Kreitz said, arguing that fewer tests mean slower learning and development.

“Unfortunately, our adversaries very much took the opposite approach,” Kreitz said on stage. “The Chinese have tested and iterated very, very fast,…

items.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration

Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes.

This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words.

items.title: ‘Absurd’: Delta CEO says it takes longer to fly from ATL to LGA today than in the 1950s
items.summary:
Delta CEO Ed Bastian says one of his airline’s oldest routes is slower now than when it launched in the 1950s, and it’s “absurd.”

“Today, it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd,” Bastian told Fortune’ s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum on Monday. 

His complaint lands days after the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide grounding of flights last week put the country’s congested air traffic control system back in the spotlight. Bastian said fixing it would bring ticket prices down by letting airlines add flights, but modernization can’t happen without investment, which doesn’t seem likely when the data-center buildout is diverting trillions in capital. 

“We can’t even get $50 billion to fix our skies, which affects all of us at a much higher level than any individual data center,” Bastian said. 

Airplanes have become more advanced since the one equipped for the world’s first scheduled commercial flight from St. Petersburg to Tampa over a century ago . By Bastian’s account, the system they fly through hasn’t kept up.

Delta is also grappling with airfare pricing after the Iran war’s pressure on jet fuel prices squeezed the airline industry , and it has passed much of that cost onto consumers. Bastian said Delta’s tickets are 15% to 20% higher year-over-year because of jet fuel, adding that this wouldn’t have been possible to do if there wasn’t sufficient demand.

“We would not be able to generate that type of pricing if we didn’t have a consumer that was…

items.title: At 17, South Carolina-bound GG Banks is building a brand before her first college game
items.summary:
Jezelle “GG” Banks doesn’t turn 18 until Nov. 27, but she already has a logo.

The senior at The St. James Academy, just outside Washington, D.C., is a five-star guard ranked No. 4 in the class of 2027 and committed to South Carolina, the No. 1 team in the AP poll. She’s as at home slicing past defenders as she is hosting long livestreams on social media.

Banks is also building a business. In a growing number of states, high school athletes can now be paid for their name, image, and likeness (NIL), just like college athletes. In an exclusive interview with Fortune , she revealed her personal logo publicly for the first time.

“I love it! It really fits me,” Banks said. “Everything in the logo has special meaning to me. I think the logo speaks to my personality—spikes of energy boosting everything, and then towards the bottom you’ve got a dollar sign, because, of course, banks.”

Logo Design & Branding: THE·TEAM 

The dollar sign plays on her last name. Banks worked on the design with her agency, THE·TEAM , the sports and entertainment firm formerly known as Wasserman. Coming just weeks before her 18th birthday, it’s a birthday present of sorts.

“This was a dream,” Banks said. THE·TEAM showed her mockups of the logo on sneakers and in Times Square. “That’s what I envisioned when I was younger, me having the logo.”

Building who she was on the court 

Custom logos are still rare among high school players, but Banks has been dreaming big for a while.

“I saw this coming a little bit, not just for me, but I think just the women’s era—people paying more attention to women’s…

items.title: Delta CEO Ed Bastian believes ‘human error’ and faulty equipment led to FAA ground stop
items.summary:
Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian thinks Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop came from “a combination of faulty equipment, coupled with human error.” He dismissed other explanations as currently lacking evidence. “There’s no evidence that there’s [an] AI trigger. There’s no evidence that there’s cyber at play.”

Bastian, speaking with Fortune’ s Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, said he has no information beyond what has been reported. “We’ll find out when it comes in,” he said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, canceling roughly 12,500 flights that day and thousands more on Saturday. It was the first nationwide stop since a January 2023 system outage, and only the second since 9/11.

What led to the FAA ground stop 

Bastian said he has talked to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and that Duffy “has been very transparent.” Duffy has said the trouble started during a copper-to-fiber switch at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Ark. A router at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, then “started to flood our system.” Contractor L3Harris did the installation, and Duffy has asked publicly whether the fault was the install or the router itself. L3Harris says it is supporting the investigation. Bedford said there was “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related.”

items.title: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth
items.summary:
Every CEO I talk to has an AI savings plan. Almost none have an AI revenue plan.

Savings matter. But an AI strategy that stops there is incomplete.

Across 50 years of entrepreneurship, I’ve helped create more than 175 companies. I’ve watched successive technology waves play out the same way. The first instinct is to use the new tool to do the old things cheaper. The companies that win use it to do new things. Electricity didn’t just lower factory power bills; it let factories be rebuilt around the assembly line. The internet didn’t just cut the cost of mailing catalogs; it created Amazon .

An EY-Parthenon survey published in April 2026 found that 63% of growth leaders at large U.S. companies said their organizations were using AI primarily for efficiency and productivity. Just 7% cited diversifying revenue streams. McKinsey’s 2026 research finds that AI high performers pursue growth or innovation alongside efficiency.

In a 2025 study of software and reasoning tasks, METR found that the length of tasks AI agents could complete with 50% reliability had been doubling roughly every seven months. Those lengths reflect how long the tasks take human experts.

AI is making ideas more abundant and early experimentation less expensive. For software-based concepts, it can help teams research a market, write and test code, and build an initial prototype before committing a larger team and budget. The hard part remains choosing the right opportunities, validating demand, and turning them into viable businesses. Established companies can draw on existing expertise and capabilities…
items.t: Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth

items.title: Meet the Sweetgreen managers who could make $200,000 training the chain’s next generation of restaurateurs
items.summary:
Ramsess Salazar was 20 when he left Caracas, Venezuela, alone in 1999. When he arrived in Minnesota, he missed the family dinners he grew up with, so he started cooking for his friends. That eventually turned into culinary school, which led to a stint in fine dining, and then a job offer from Sweetgreen in 2018 that sent him to Boston.

Eight years later, he runs the chain’s bustling Fulton Market store in Chicago and trains the managers who will run its next restaurants. Last month, he got a call from Sweetgreen CEO Jonathan Neman explaining that his work is coming with a new compensation package.

“I couldn’t believe it,” Salazar told Fortune . What surprised him more was that the company’s leaders called him personally: “Which CEO really does that?”

Starting in the first quarter of 2027, Sweetgreen’s top managers can earn over $200k in total compensation includes salary, revenue-share, and equity. The top tier is open to “Head Coaches,” Sweetgreen’s name for general managers, who have at least three years with the company and lead its busiest stores. COO Jason Cochran estimated that 10% to 12% of head coaches meet all the criteria. Managers chosen for its restaurateur program, like Salazar, also get $10,000 for every employee they develop into a head coach, with no cap.

Ramsess Salazar outside his Chicago location. Sweetgreen 

“The idea is now you’re a talent factory,” Neman told Fortune . “You’ve demonstrated you’re good at your job. Now can you train someone else? Future leaders? Train them up, and we’ll pay you $10,000 every single time you do it.”

‘100 grand…
items.t: Meet the Sweetgreen managers who could make $200,000 training the chain’s next generation of restaurateurs
